newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FEATURE - NZ's Progressive on road to recovery.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - NZ's Progressive on road to recovery.

text.p: New Zealand's biggest supermarket chain Progressive Enterprises Ltd is on the road to recovery a year after chief executive Graeme Kelly embarked on restructuring.
When Kelly started in February 1996, Progressive had just completed its half year, producing a NZ$2.2 million (US$1.55 million) profit that was significantly below expectations.
True to form, the year to July 1996 turned out dismally. The company, 57 percent-owned by Australia's Foodland Associated, reported a profit of just NZ$3.55 million, down 81.4 percent.
WHAT WENT WRONG?
It had become obvious to the company in late 1995 that all was not well, prompting the board to stop all capital expenditure programmes.
But because of the number of capital works in train at the time, existing projects still needed to be completed and funded.
The consequences of that ran through into the early months of 1996, which saw interest bearing debt topping out at NZ$210 million.
At the same time, profits were dropping like a stone, forcing a brief breach of Progressive's interest rate covenants.
Then there was the question of what to do with the Georgie Pie fast food chain, which was losing about NZ$8.0 million a year and which had become the single biggest drain on profits.
Georgie Pie, which began in the mid 1970s, had fallen prey to the proliferation of multi-national fast food operators and had expanded too quickly.
In supermarkets, some of Progressive's businesses had retained their competitive culture, even though they were now under one umbrella.
Kelly said the company's volume purchasing opportunities had in the past been "confused and compromised". Progressive had become too fragmented, undermining its natural advantage as a bulk buyer.
RECOVERY PLAN

One of the first steps taken by Kelly, who like many of the new managers had been with the company before, was to restructure the logistical side through the formation of The Supply Chain, which took responsibility for warehousing and product distribution to Progressive's operating businesses.
Next on the agenda was to terminate Progressive's involvement with Southway Properties, in which it had a 20 percent interest but only 10 percent representation.

Seventeen Georgie Pie sites were then sold to McDonalds for NZ$25.5 million. Of the 15 restaurants left, four have leases that will run out in less than two years and they will not be renewed, bringing the core number of businesses down to 11.
Progressive has not yet decided to quit Georgie Pie altogether, but Kelly said the McDonalds deal has stimulated interest in the remaining sites.
MANAGEMENT
Management had previously been divided into three groups -- one for Foodtown, another for Countdown and Three Guys, with the third group charged with buying nationally.
"This meant a fragmentation of activities. It tended to lead to a continuation of the competition between the businesses that existed prior to common ownership being established," Kelly said.
There were also vast inefficiencies in having to repeat processes two or three times through each business. It also made it confusing for suppliers.

In July, a single administrative structure was formed for managing the supermarkets, which had eliminated the competitive behaviour, established collaboration, removed inefficiencies and created a simple organisation.
THE SITUATION NOW
Major divestments had created significant cash flow and had assisted in the run down of debt to the tune of NZ$70-80 million.
The capital works programme has been completed and capital expenditure has dried up.
Restoration of profitabilty had created an "earned" cash flow.
Asset sales had altered the balance sheet dramatically, meaning further divestments were no longer an imperative.
THE FUTURE
Kelly said manufacturing was going through a rationalisation, as evidenced by the plethora of companies concentrating manufacturing facilities in either Australia or New Zealand, but not both.
Manufacturers were also turning their back on what he called the "milk run" system of delivering goods directly to retailers.

"This will lead us, in many cases, to buying the product in Australia and shipping it here ourselves, that way taking the whole of the very high-cost, low-volume, inefficient handling cost burden out of the system," he said.
The company is to institute a "world class" project that will encompass education, adopting processes and practices and software selection, all reinforcing a "chain store" mentality.
On the drawing board is a plan to spend NZ$15 million over two years on checkout technologies.
Once the computing infrastructure is installed, Progressive plans to dispose of its multiple operating platforms and systems throughout Rattrays, Countdown and Foodtown.
It also plans to reduce the number of supermarket brands and to close duplicated stores.
Then there was the issue of "unbundling" the several distinctly different businesses of Rattrays. To that end, Progressive will proceed with three initiatives over the next few months.
At this point of the "restoration and reformation" programme, Kelly said Progressive expects to exceed analysts' first half forecasts of a net profit of NZ$6.0-7.5 million.

"If you work those numbers through...analysts' forecasts of NZ$15-20 million this year and $25-30 million in 1997/8, you are getting the order of magnitude of improvement that we are working to achieve and believe is realistic to achieve."
